---
id: 00
type: facilitator
title: Opening
duration: 10 min
---

## what you say

Start without slides if you can. Just talk.

"Before we do anything else, I want to ask you a question. Think about the last time AI showed up in your work—not something you went looking for. Something that was already there. A recommendation. A flagged record. A suggested code. A pre-populated field.

Who prompted that?

Most of what gets called AI literacy assumes you're the one asking. You type something, the AI responds, you decide what to do with it. That's one kind of AI. It's not the only kind—and for most of you, it may not even be the main kind.

Today we're going to work with the kind you ask. The compositional kind. Prompts, responses, judgment. Not because it's more important than the AI that's already in your workflows—but because understanding this side makes you better at reading the other side.

By the end of this workshop you'll have worked with at least two different AI models on real HIM scenarios. You'll have made them argue with each other. And you'll have a small workbench—artifacts you generated, saved, and can take back to your organization.

That's the goal. Let's start."

## what you don't say

- Don't explain what an LLM is. They'll see it.
- Don't apologize for the tech. If something breaks, that's data.
- Don't promise the AI will be impressive. It won't always be.

## notes

The phrase "who prompted that?" is the load-bearing move. It plants the directive/compositional distinction without naming it. You'll return to it in the wrap.

---
id: 01
type: facilitator
title: Icebreaker + Infrastructure
duration: 20-25 min
---

## purpose

Get everyone into a model. Surface platform variance immediately. Establish the Drive folder as home base. Seed the "two models are better than one" lesson before the first real sprint.

## step 1: get them connected (5 min)

Show the QR code or say the URL: **tiny.cc/nyhima**

"Open that on your laptop or tablet. Everything you need today lives there—scenarios, system prompts, instructions. You don't need to install anything. You just need a browser and access to one of these: ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini. If you have all three, even better."

Circulate. Table captains help neighbors. Don't wait for 100%—start the icebreaker when most tables are ready.

## step 2: the icebreaker prompt (8 min)

"Before we do anything else, I want you to try something simple. Open your model. Paste this prompt exactly as written."

**ICEBREAKER PROMPT** (also in Drive as system-prompts/00-icebreaker.txt):

> You are an expert in health information management. In exactly one sentence, describe what HIM professionals do—written for a hospital board member who has never heard the term.

"Run it. Read what you get. Now—if you have a second model open, run it there too."

Wait 2–3 minutes. Then ask the room:

- "What did your model say?"
- "Did anyone get something surprising?"
- "Did two models give you different sentences?"

Take 3–4 responses. Point out the variance. That's the first lesson: **same prompt, different models, different outputs.** The model is a variable, not a constant.

## step 3: introduce the system prompt library (5 min)

"In the Drive folder you'll find a folder called system-prompts. These are pre-written instructions that change how the model behaves before you ask your real question. Think of them as lenses. We'll use them throughout the day."

"System prompt 1 makes the model a skeptical reviewer. System prompt 2 makes it a plain-language translator. System prompt 3 makes it argue the other side. We'll talk about which one to use when."

Demo on the shared screen: open system-prompt-01.txt, copy it, paste it into a model as the first message, then ask a follow-up. Show that the model's behavior changes.

## step 4: orient to the day (2 min)

"We have three buckets of scenarios—Data, Policy, and Judgment. Each table will work through one bucket at a time together. You pick your scenario within the bucket. You can do one or four—your call. After each bucket we debrief as a room."

"At the end of the day, you have whatever you saved. That's your workbench. It's yours."

## notes

The icebreaker prompt is deliberately easy. The point isn't the answer—it's the variance. If two models at the same table give meaningfully different sentences, that's worth more than anything you could say about model differences.

If someone doesn't have access to any model, pair them with someone who does. Don't spend more than 2 minutes solving individual tech problems—keep moving.

---
id: 02
type: facilitator
title: Sprint 1 — Data
duration: 35 min (25 sprint + 10 debrief)
---

## intro (2 min)

"First bucket: Data. These scenarios give you a table or a set of numbers—the kind of thing that lands in your inbox with a question attached. Your job is to read it with a model, then have a second model check the first one's work."

"Pick any scenario in the D bucket. If your table wants to split up and do different ones, go ahead. You have 25 minutes."

Point to the Drive folder: **scenarios/data/**

## the sprint cycle — post this or keep it on screen

```
1. Read your scenario situation
2. Paste the source document into Model A
3. Run the writing prompt
4. Save or copy the output
5. Open Model B (different model)
6. Paste the validation prompt
7. Paste in Model A's output
8. Compare
9. Answer the reflection question — just think it, don't write it yet
```

## what you do during the sprint

Circulate. Listen for:
- Someone surprised by what the second model caught
- Someone frustrated that both models said the same thing
- Someone who noticed the model was confidently wrong

Those are your debrief voices. Note who they are.

Ask tables: "Which model are you on?" Nudge anyone who hasn't switched models yet.

## debrief (10 min)

Open with: **"Did the second model catch something the first one missed?"**

Take 3–4 responses. Then push:

- "Did anyone have both models agree—and then realize they were both wrong?"
- "Where did your own knowledge have to step in?"

Land the lesson: **Two models are better than one. But two models plus your expertise is better than either.**

Don't over-explain. Let the room's experience carry it. Move to Sprint 2.

## if tables finish early

Point them to the next D scenario. Or ask: "Try the same scenario with a different system prompt. Does the output change?"

## notes

The data scenarios are the most accessible—good place to build confidence before Policy and Judgment raise the stakes. If the room is slow to start, do a quick demo of D1 on the shared screen: paste the source, run the writing prompt, show the output. 90 seconds. Then hand it back to them.

---
id: 03
type: facilitator
title: Sprint 2 — Policy
duration: 35 min (25 sprint + 10 debrief)
---

## intro (2 min)

"Second bucket: Policy. These scenarios give you actual regulatory language—HIPAA, CMS, ONC. Your job is to have the model interpret it and make it usable. Then have a second model check whether the first one got the law right."

"Work in pairs this time. One person runs the writing prompt, the other runs the validation prompt. Compare before we debrief."

Point to: **scenarios/policy/**

## what shifts from sprint 1

The stakes are higher. Legal language is precise in ways that matter. A model that smooths over an exception or misreads a timeline can produce guidance that gets someone in trouble. That's the lesson—but don't say it yet. Let them find it.

## what you do during the sprint

Listen for the moment someone says "that's not quite right" or "it left out the part about..."

That's your debrief voice.

Watch for pairs where one person has domain expertise the other doesn't. The expert is doing the validation the model should be doing. Name that in the debrief.

## debrief (10 min)

Open with: **"Where did the model get the legal language wrong—or not wrong exactly, but... soft?"**

Push:
- "Did it add qualifications that made it useless?"
- "Did it drop a distinction that actually matters?"
- "Would you hand what it produced to a colleague—or a physician—without editing it?"

Then land the harder question: **"If you didn't already know this regulation, how would you have known the model got it wrong?"**

Let that sit for a moment. That's the point. A model that sounds authoritative about law is a specific kind of dangerous.

Connect briefly—don't lecture—to directive AI: "This is what happens when the AI is already in the workflow. The model interpreted the policy before you read it. You got a recommendation. Was it right?"

Move to Sprint 3.

## notes

P4 (Breach Notification Clock) tends to generate the most friction—the four-factor test is concrete enough that people notice when the model applies it sloppily. If a table seems stuck, nudge them toward P4.

P2 (Minimum Necessary) is the most immediately practical for most HIM professionals. Good for tables that want something they can use Monday morning.

---
id: 04
type: facilitator
title: Sprint 3 — Judgment
duration: 35 min (25 sprint + 10 debrief)
---

## intro (2 min)

"Last bucket: Judgment. These scenarios don't have clean answers. They have competing values, incomplete information, and real professional stakes. Your job is to see what the model does when you ask it to decide something."

"Work as a full table. One person runs the prompts—on their own screen or on a shared device. Everyone watches. Then talk."

Point to: **scenarios/judgment/**

## what shifts from sprint 2

This isn't about whether the model got the facts right. It's about whether the model will own a decision—and what it does instead. Most participants will have an opinion about these scenarios. The model will perform balance. That gap is the lesson.

## recommended scenario for full-table discussion

**J3 — The AI Note in the Chart** works best for collective discussion because it puts participants in the position of using an AI to reason about an AI mistake. The reflection question names that directly.

**J2 — The Record Request That Worries You** works well if the table has clinical background. The legal vs. ethical distinction hits hard.

**J4 — The Vendor Who Wants Your Data** is the most immediately relevant to organizational life and generates strong opinions.

## what you do during the sprint

Less circulating, more watching. Let the table run. If a table goes quiet after the model output, ask: "Do you agree with that?"

If a table is debating among themselves rather than engaging the model, that's fine—let it run another minute, then ask them to run the validation prompt and see if the second model changes the conversation.

## debrief (10 min)

Open with: **"Did the model decide—or did it hand it back to you?"**

Push:
- "Was that useful or frustrating?"
- "If you followed what the model said, who's accountable for the outcome?"
- "Did anyone notice the model was careful not to be wrong—rather than trying to be right?"

For J3 tables: "You just used an AI to analyze a problem caused by an AI. Did it acknowledge that? Should it have?"

Land the lesson: **The model won't own it. Someone has to. In your organization, that someone is you.**

Don't rush the close. This is where the day's learning consolidates.

## notes

The judgment scenarios can generate real disagreement at the table—that's good. Don't resolve it. The point is that these scenarios require human judgment precisely because reasonable professionals disagree. If the model gave a tidy answer, ask: "Would you be comfortable if your name was on that?"

---
id: 05
type: facilitator
title: Wrap
duration: 10-15 min
---

## what you say

"At the beginning I asked: who prompted that?

You've spent three hours on the version of AI where you do the prompting. You've seen what it can do—and what it won't do. It catches things. It misses things. It sounds confident when it should hedge and hedges when it should decide. Two models are better than one. Your expertise is what makes either of them useful.

The AI already in your workflows—the one that flags records, suggests codes, surfaces recommendations before you've formed your own opinion—that one is harder to interrogate. But now you have a practice for it. You know what questions to ask. You know what to hand to a second model. You know that 'the AI said so' is not a complete answer.

What you built today is yours. Whatever you saved—outputs, conversations, notes—that's a workbench. Lightweight, portable, yours. The scenarios and system prompts stay in the Drive folder. There are twelve scenarios total; we ran through three buckets today. The rest are there when you want them.

If you want to go further—if your organization is trying to figure out what AI literacy means for HIM practice, for training, for policy—that's the work we're doing at SUNY Poly. The link is in the folder."

## what you don't say

- Don't summarize every lesson. They lived them.
- Don't end with "AI is changing everything." They know. They're tired of hearing it.
- Don't undersell what they built. They made something today.

## the one thing to leave them with

"Literacy isn't knowing how to prompt. It's knowing when to push back."

## logistics close (2 min)

- Drive folder stays live — tiny.cc/nyhima
- System prompt library is there to use and share
- SUNY Poly AIX Center: sunypolyaix.github.io
- Questions, follow-up, collaboration: steve@sunypoly.edu

## notes

If time allows, ask one final question to the room before you close: "What's one thing you're going to do differently on Monday?" Don't collect answers—just let people sit with it for 10 seconds. Then close.

---

# System Prompt Library
## NYHIMA Workshop — June 7, 2026

Copy any of these as your first message to a model before running a scenario prompt.
Changing the system prompt changes how the model behaves. That's the point.

---

## SP-00: Icebreaker

> You are an expert in health information management.

*Use for: the opening icebreaker only.*

---

## SP-01: Skeptical Reviewer

> You are a rigorous analyst reviewing AI-generated professional documents. Your job is not to be helpful—it is to find problems. Identify what is missing, what is assumed without evidence, what is legally imprecise, and what a professional would immediately question. Do not soften your critique. Do not suggest improvements unless asked. Just find what's wrong.

*Use for: validation prompts in any bucket. Makes the second model harder on the first.*

---

## SP-02: Plain Language Translator

> You are a health information professional who specializes in making complex regulatory and clinical content accessible to non-experts. Translate technical content into plain language suitable for clinical staff with no HIM background. Avoid jargon. Use short sentences. If something cannot be simplified without losing critical meaning, say so explicitly.

*Use for: Policy bucket writing prompts. Good for P1 and P2.*

---

## SP-03: Devil's Advocate

> You are a professional trained to argue the opposing position. Whatever argument or recommendation you are given, identify the strongest case against it. Do not agree with the position you are given. Do not hedge. Make the best possible counterargument, even if you personally find it unpersuasive.

*Use for: Judgment bucket. Run the writing prompt output through this to see the other side.*

---

## SP-04: Executive Communicator

> You are a senior health information professional preparing briefings for hospital executives. Your outputs are concise, evidence-based, and action-oriented. Lead with the bottom line. Avoid passive voice. Every claim must be supported by the data or document you have been given—do not introduce information that isn't there.

*Use for: Data bucket writing prompts. Good for D1, D2, D3.*

---

## SP-05: Patient Advocate

> You are reviewing professional documents and decisions from the perspective of the patient whose information is involved. Ask: What would the patient want to know? What has been left out that affects them? Where does this decision prioritize organizational interests over patient interests? Be specific.

*Use for: Judgment bucket validation prompts. Especially good for J2 and J3.*

---

## SP-06: Neutral Summarizer

> You are a neutral summarizer. Summarize the document or output you are given as accurately and completely as possible. Do not editorialize. Do not add analysis. Do not draw conclusions the document doesn't support. If something is ambiguous, say it is ambiguous.

*Use for: creating synthesis artifacts to pass between models.*

---

## Notes on use

- Paste the system prompt as your first message, then paste the scenario prompt in your next message.
- Or combine them: paste the system prompt + scenario prompt together as one message.
- Try the same scenario with two different system prompts. The variance is the lesson.
- These prompts work across Claude, ChatGPT, and Gemini—with different results.

# Reading and Writing with AI
## Facilitator Deck — NYHIMA Workshop | June 7, 2026 | 1:00–4:00 PM

---

## SLIDE 00 — Title / Holding Slide
*(on screen as participants arrive)*

**Reading and Writing with AI**
Using Large Language Models in Professional Practice

Steve Schneider | SUNY Poly AIX Center
NYHIMA | June 7, 2026

Everything lives at: **tiny.cc/nyhima**

---

## SLIDE 01 — Opening Question
*(10 min)*

**Who prompted that?**

Think about the last time AI showed up in your work—not something you went looking for.

- A recommendation
- A flagged record
- A suggested code
- A pre-populated field

*Who asked for it?*

---

## SLIDE 02 — Two Kinds of AI

**The kind you ask.**
You prompt → AI responds → you decide.

**The kind that asks you.**
AI surfaces a recommendation → you respond → you decide.

> Today we work on the first kind—because understanding it makes you better at reading the second.

---

## SLIDE 03 — What You'll Build Today

By 4:00 PM you will have:

- Worked with at least **two different AI models**
- Run real HIM scenarios through both
- Made them argue with each other
- Saved artifacts you can take back to your organization

That's your **workbench**. It's yours.

---

## SLIDE 04 — Get Connected
*(Icebreaker + Infrastructure | 20–25 min)*

**Open: tiny.cc/nyhima**

You need:
- A laptop or tablet
- Access to ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini
- A browser. That's it.

*Table captains: help your neighbors get in.*

---

## SLIDE 05 — Icebreaker Prompt
*(leave on screen while they run it)*

Open your model. Paste this exactly:

> *You are an expert in health information management. In exactly one sentence, describe what HIM professionals do—written for a hospital board member who has never heard the term.*

If you have a second model open: **run it there too.**

---

## SLIDE 06 — What You Just Saw

Same prompt. Different models. Different outputs.

**The model is a variable, not a constant.**

That's the first lesson. We'll keep building on it.

---

## SLIDE 07 — System Prompts
*(leave on screen during demo)*

System prompts are instructions that change how the model behaves **before** you ask your real question.

| Code | Name | Use for |
|------|------|---------|
| SP-01 | Skeptical Reviewer | Validation — any bucket |
| SP-02 | Plain Language Translator | Policy writing |
| SP-03 | Devil's Advocate | Judgment bucket |
| SP-04 | Executive Communicator | Data writing |
| SP-05 | Patient Advocate | Judgment validation |
| SP-06 | Neutral Summarizer | Moving artifacts between models |

Full prompts: **tiny.cc/nyhima → system-prompts/**

---

## SLIDE 08 — The Day's Structure

Three buckets. Three sprints. One debrief each.

| Bucket | Scenarios | What you're testing |
|--------|-----------|---------------------|
| **Data** | D1–D4 | Does the second model catch what the first missed? |
| **Policy** | P1–P4 | Does the model get the legal language right? |
| **Judgment** | J1–J4 | Will the model decide—or hand it back to you? |

You pick your scenario within each bucket.

---

## SLIDE 09 — The Sprint Cycle
*(leave on screen for all three sprints)*

```
1. Read the situation
2. Paste the source document into Model A
3. Run the writing prompt → read the output → save it
4. Open Model B (different model)
5. Paste the validation prompt → paste in Model A's output
6. Compare — where do they diverge?
7. Reflect — sit with the reflection question
```

---

## SLIDE 10 — Sprint 1: Data
*(35 min | 25 sprint + 10 debrief)*

**Bucket D — pick any scenario**

| ID | Title |
|----|-------|
| D1 | The Discharge Data |
| D2 | The Coding Accuracy Audit |
| D3 | The ROI Request Surge |
| D4 | The Duplicate MRN Problem |

*tiny.cc/nyhima → scenarios/data/*

**You have 25 minutes. Go.**

---

## SLIDE 11 — Sprint 1 Working
*(on screen during sprint)*

**Sprint 1 — Data** | 25 min

*Sprint cycle on Slide 09*

**Try:** SP-04 (Executive Communicator) for writing prompts
**Try:** SP-01 (Skeptical Reviewer) for validation prompts

*Finished early? Try the same scenario with a different system prompt.*

---

## SLIDE 12 — Sprint 1 Debrief

**Did the second model catch something the first one missed?**

- Did both models agree—and were they both wrong?
- Where did your own knowledge have to step in?

> Two models are better than one.
> Two models plus your expertise is better than either.

---

## SLIDE 13 — Sprint 2: Policy
*(35 min | 25 sprint + 10 debrief)*

**Bucket P — work in pairs**
One person: writing prompt. Other person: validation prompt.

| ID | Title |
|----|-------|
| P1 | The Information Blocking Rule |
| P2 | The Minimum Necessary Standard |
| P3 | The Retention Policy Gap |
| P4 | The Breach Notification Clock |

*tiny.cc/nyhima → scenarios/policy/*

---

## SLIDE 14 — Sprint 2 Working
*(on screen during sprint)*

**Sprint 2 — Policy** | 25 min

*Sprint cycle on Slide 09*

**Try:** SP-02 (Plain Language Translator) for writing prompts
**Try:** SP-01 (Skeptical Reviewer) for validation prompts

*Stuck? P4 (Breach Notification) generates the most friction. P2 (Minimum Necessary) is the most immediately practical.*

---

## SLIDE 15 — Sprint 2 Debrief

**Where did the model get the legal language wrong—or not wrong exactly, but... soft?**

- Did it add qualifications that made it useless?
- Did it drop a distinction that actually matters?

**If you didn't already know this regulation, how would you have known the model got it wrong?**

*A model that sounds authoritative about law is a specific kind of dangerous.*

## SLIDE 16 — Sprint 3: Judgment
*(35 min | 25 sprint + 10 debrief)*

*Not sure where to start? J3 (AI Note in the Chart) works well for full-table discussion. J4 (Vendor Data) generates strong opinions.*

---

## SLIDE 18 — Sprint 3 Debrief

**Did the model decide—or did it hand it back to you?**

- Was that useful or frustrating?
- If you followed what the model said, who's accountable for the outcome?
- Did anyone notice the model was careful not to be wrong—rather than trying to be right?

> The model won't own it. Someone has to.
> In your organization, that someone is you.

---

## SLIDE 19 — Wrap
*(10–15 min)*

**Who prompted that?**

You've spent three hours on the version of AI where you do the prompting.

The AI already in your workflows—the one that flags records, suggests codes, surfaces recommendations before you've formed your own opinion—that one is harder to interrogate.

22 slides. A few structural decisions worth flagging:

**Slides designed to stay on screen during work sessions** — 09 (Sprint Cycle), 11, 14, 17 (bucket working slides) are explicitly meant to sit there while participants run scenarios. They include a pointer back to the cycle slide and a nudge on which system prompts to try.

**Holding slides at both ends** — 00 is pre-session; 22 (Close) can sit through Q&A and any lingering conversation.

**The "who prompted that?" call-back** is bookended on slides 01 and 19, same as the opening/wrap structure in the facilitator notes.

**Timing appendix** at the end with cumulative clock — handy for a second monitor or a glance when you're losing track mid-session. Notes a ~25-minute buffer built into the 3 hours, which is realistic given the icebreaker tech chaos.

One thing missing that you may want to add: if you're actually running this in a slide tool (Keynote, PowerPoint, Google Slides), the working slides (11, 14, 17) would benefit from the sprint cycle duplicated inline rather than pointing back to slide 09. Easy to do if you want a version for conversion.

i want everyone to have two models: chatgpt, gemini, claude, pick 2 or pick all three.

why evenintroduce the compositon / directive?

i didn't do any level set with the nyhima crowd: i should

so all three cycles: slide 9: just one model to another? that's boring!!!!

Good catches, all three. Let me think through each:

**Two models (pick 2 or all 3)** — easy fix, the slide just needs to name the three and say "at least two open at all times."

**Why introduce compositional/directive at all** — you're right to question it. The workshop *is* compositional, so the distinction is either throat-clearing or it's doing real work. The only reason to name it is the wrap payoff: "the AI already in your workflows did something different." But you could earn that without the terminology. Do you want to keep the concept but drop the jargon, or drop it entirely and just open with the "who prompted that?" question and let the wrap land on its own?

**No level-set with NYHIMA crowd** — what do you want them to know before they start? The Tuesday talk has the full HIM-specific argument (domains, directive AI in their workflows). The workshop has been assuming they already have that frame. Without it, Sprint 1 might work fine, but the Policy and Judgment debriefs depend on participants feeling the professional stakes. What's the gap you felt — they didn't know why this mattered for *their field specifically*, or something more basic?

**Sprint cycle boring** — "paste into Model A, then Model B" is a validation structure, which is useful but yeah, flat. What would make it not boring? A few directions:

- Models in *competition* rather than sequence (run the same prompt in all three simultaneously, compare)
- Models in *dialogue* (paste what Claude said into ChatGPT and ask "where is this wrong")
- Models with *different personas* (same scenario, SP-03 on one, SP-05 on another — not checking each other, arguing)
- Participant as *judge* (both outputs on screen, you decide who got it right and why)

Which of those feels right, or is it something else?

drop it entirely. right now, open who prompted that. the level set is to assess gaps and skills and help me with language and tone. i've done that with a quick incluass survey and mmento or excel fill in the form

Got it. So the opening stays exactly as written — "who prompted that?" no framing, no terminology, just the question.

For the level-set: you ran a quick in-class survey (Mentimeter or Excel form) before the workshop, and you want a slide or two that helps you read the room and adjust language/tone based on what comes back. 

A few questions to make that useful:

**What did you ask them?** If I can see the survey questions (or you describe them), I can draft slide language that responds to the likely variance — e.g., if half the room has never opened ChatGPT, the icebreaker needs different framing than if most are daily users.

**When does the survey happen?** Before they arrive (pre-session email), or the first thing they do when they sit down? That changes where it fits in the deck.

**What do you want to do with the results live?** Options:
- You read the room silently and adjust tone on the fly (no slide needed, just your read)
- You show aggregate results briefly and name the variance ("half of you use these daily, half have never tried — good, that's exactly the room I want")
- You use it to sort tables by experience level before sprints start

The "show the variance" move is the most interesting one — it does double duty as a level-set *and* an early demonstration that heterogeneity in the room is a feature, not a problem. Mirrors the "same prompt, different outputs" lesson you're already building toward.

What did the survey ask?
the task has to be different. data / compare two models / have one critique the other. fine.  Now do two diff things in policy and the third example

So the three sprints need structurally different tasks, not just different content. Something like:

**Sprint 1 (Data):** Two models, one critiques the other. You're already there.

**Sprint 2 (Policy):** What's the second move? A few options:
- Same regulatory text, two models get *different system prompts* — one translates for clinical staff, one translates for executives. Compare what got dropped in each translation.
- One model interprets the regulation, second model *argues it got it wrong* (SP-03 as the adversary, not a neutral checker)
- Two models, but they get *different excerpts* of the same regulation — then you surface what each missed because it didn't see the whole thing

**Sprint 3 (Judgment):** Third distinct structure. Options:
- Models in *sequence*: Model A makes a recommendation, you paste it into Model B and say "a colleague gave me this advice — push back on it." Human never reveals it's AI-generated.
- *You* decide first, then run the model, then compare your reasoning to the model's
- Models get *different roles* baked in (SP-03 vs SP-05 — devil's advocate vs patient advocate) and you watch them disagree

What's your instinct on Policy and Judgment? And is the Data structure "run writing prompt in both models simultaneously, then compare" — or still sequential with the second critiquing the first?
dont have to be two models

Right. The constraint is interesting tasks, not model count.

So reframe: each sprint has a different **cognitive task structure**.

**Sprint 1 (Data):** Two models, one critiques the other. The task is *verification* — can a second reader catch what the first missed?

**Sprint 2 (Policy):** One model, but the task is *translation under constraint* — take this regulatory language and make it usable for [audience]. Then you evaluate whether the translation holds up. The interesting move is the human doing the evaluation, not a second model.

**Sprint 3 (Judgment):** You decide first. Write your own position, then run the model, then compare. The task is *self-confrontation* — where did you and the model diverge, and who's right?

That third one is the sharpest move in the room. Most participants have never been asked to commit to a position *before* seeing what the AI says. It makes the model's hedge visible in a completely different way — not "the model hedged" but "I took a side and the model wouldn't."

Does that structure work? And for Policy — is the evaluator always the human, or do you want a third-model move available for tables that want it?
why 3? what is the point? to get them to commit first? to illustarte a particular kind of cognitive bias?

The point is automation bias — specifically the pre-exposure version. If you see the model's answer first, you anchor to it. You think you're evaluating it but you're actually just ratifying or slightly adjusting it. Committing first breaks that.

It's the most direct demonstration of why directive AI is dangerous that you can run in a workshop. The AI in their workflows already did this to them — surfaced a recommendation before they formed an opinion. The sprint recreates that failure condition and then inverts it so they can feel the difference.

So the question is whether that's the lesson you want Sprint 3 to land. If yes, the structure is: commit first, then run the model, then ask "did you change your mind — and why?"

But if the Judgment bucket lesson is something else — "the model won't own a decision" or "reasonable professionals disagree and the model performs false balance" — then commit-first is the wrong structure. It answers a different question.

What do you want them to walk out of Sprint 3 knowing?

i want them to walk out of the workshop knowing: prompting matter, more models matter. you need to wkr hard to get good stuff out of the model. many prompt, many refines, improves the output. perhaps: it is worth exactly what you put into it, and those reading your "slop" can feel it

That's a clean through-line. The workshop is about *effort and iteration*, not model magic.

Which means the three sprints should each demonstrate a different dimension of that same lesson:

**Sprint 1 (Data):** More models catches more. One pass isn't enough — a second reader finds what the first missed. *Lesson: one prompt, one model is the floor, not the ceiling.*

**Sprint 2 (Policy):** More prompts, more refinement. Run it, read it, push back, run it again. The first output is a draft, not an answer. *Lesson: iteration improves the output — but you have to know what "better" looks like.*

**Sprint 3 (Judgment):** You get out what you put in. Lazy prompt gets performed balance. A prompt that commits, that has specificity, that has your actual reasoning in it — gets something harder and more useful back. *Lesson: slop in, slop out. Your expertise is the input that makes the output worth anything.*

And the wrap closes it: "the people reading what you produce with AI can feel when you phoned it in. So can you."

Does that feel like the right spine? And is Sprint 2's lesson "iteration" or something sharper — like "you have to already know enough to recognize when it's wrong"?
not sure about 2. it is both, emphasis on iteration. that is the right spine. what do we have to do? rgenerate all the scenarios?

No. The scenarios are good — the content holds. What needs to change is the **task structure** layered on top of them.

Right now every scenario has the same shape: writing prompt → validation prompt → reflection. That's the part that needs to vary across the three sprints to carry the spine.

Specifically:

**Sprint 1** — task structure already works for "more models catches more." Minor tweak: make explicit that they run the writing prompt in *both* models simultaneously before comparing, not sequentially. Changes the feel from validation to comparison.

**Sprint 2** — task structure needs a new layer: after the first output, they have to push back and run it again. At least one refinement cycle built into the sprint. The validation prompt stays but it comes after iteration, not instead of it.

**Sprint 3** — task structure needs the most work. The writing prompt has to require more of them — not "help me think through this" but something that forces them to put their own reasoning in first. The prompt structure inside the scenarios has to change.

So: not regenerating scenarios. Regenerating the **sprint structure slides** and **revising the writing prompts in the J bucket** to demand more input from the participant before the model responds.

Want to start with the sprint structure slides to lock the spine, then go scenario by scenario on the J bucket writing prompts?
but in three refinement cycles.

Right. So the spine is actually:

**Sprint 1:** One prompt, two models. Compare. *More models.*

**Sprint 2:** One model, multiple prompts. Iterate. *More refinement.*

**Sprint 3:** You first, then the model, then push it. *More you.*

Each sprint isolates one variable. Together they make the argument: good output requires all three — breadth, iteration, and your own thinking as the input.

The three refinement cycles map cleanly onto that. Do you want the cycles to be:

**1 → 2 → 3** as a progression where each sprint adds the previous lesson on top — so Sprint 3 is doing all three things at once (two models, multiple prompts, you first)? 

Or do they stay isolated — each sprint demonstrates its one thing cleanly, and the synthesis happens in the wrap?
so 2 isn't multi models 3 combines both stragtegies.

Right. So:

**Sprint 1:** Two models, one prompt. *More models.*

**Sprint 2:** One model, multiple prompts. Iterate and refine. *More effort.*

**Sprint 3:** Both strategies together — multiple models, multiple prompts, and your reasoning as the fuel. *This is what good looks like.*

The wrap then names what they just did: Sprint 3 is the full practice. That's what it costs to produce something worth handing to a colleague. If you didn't do that work, they can feel it.

Do the existing scenario buckets map cleanly onto this — Data for Sprint 1, Policy for Sprint 2, Judgment for Sprint 3? Or does the assignment of buckets to sprints need to shift now that the task structures are clearer?
plus in 3, a richer starter prompt?

Yes. Sprint 3 is:

- Richer starter prompt (you put your reasoning in first)
- Multiple refinements
- Multiple models

So the J bucket writing prompts need to be rewritten — not "help me think through this" but something that requires participants to commit their own analysis before the model responds. The model is reacting to *their thinking*, not generating thinking for them to ratify.

Which means the starter prompt for J scenarios probably has a two-part structure:

1. **You write first** — your read of the situation, your instinct, your professional position. Even a few sentences.
2. **Then the prompt** — feed that into the model along with the source, ask it to stress-test, push back, find what you missed.

The model is now a critic of their thinking, not a substitute for it.

Before rewriting the J prompts: do you want the workshop to *tell* participants to write their position first as an instruction, or do you want the writing prompt itself to demand it — i.e., the prompt is structured so it doesn't work unless they fill in their reasoning?

The second is harder to write but more effective. A prompt that has a blank where their judgment goes.
i think the 2nd is prone to misinterpretation and delay

Agreed. Instruction is cleaner — tell them explicitly before they open the model: "Before you touch the keyboard, write two or three sentences about what you think should happen. On paper, in a doc, doesn't matter. Then build that into your prompt."

That's a facilitator move, not a prompt design problem. You say it in the Sprint 3 intro, it's on the working slide, and it's in the participant reference card.

So the J bucket writing prompts don't need a structural overhaul — they just need the "help me think through" framing replaced with something that assumes the participant is bringing a position. Something like "I think X. Here's my reasoning. Push back on it. What am I missing? What's the strongest case against my position?"

The prompt becomes a template with a slot they've already filled before they sit down at the model.

Ready to work through the deliverables? I'd suggest in order:

1. Revised sprint structure slides (01–04) to lock the three-sprint spine
2. Revised J bucket writing prompts (J1–J4) to match Sprint 3 expectations
3. Revised participant reference card to reflect all of it

Start with the sprint slides?
slides first

{"language": "markdown", "code": "# Reading and Writing with AI
## Facilitator Deck — NYHIMA Workshop | June 7, 2026 | 1:00–4:00 PM

---

## SLIDE 00 — Title / Holding Slide
*(on screen as participants arrive)*

**Reading and Writing with AI**
Using Large Language Models in Professional Practice

Steve Schneider | SUNY Poly AIX Center
NYHIMA | June 7, 2026

Everything lives at: **tiny.cc/nyhima**

---

## SLIDE 01 — Opening Question
*(10 min)*

**Who prompted that?**

Think about the last time AI showed up in your work—not something you went looking for.

- A recommendation
- A flagged record
- A suggested code
- A pre-populated field

*Who asked for it?*

---

## SLIDE 02 — Two Kinds of AI

**The kind you ask.**
You prompt → AI responds → you decide.

**The kind that asks you.**
AI surfaces a recommendation → you respond → you decide.

> Today we work on the first kind—because understanding it makes you better at reading the second.

---

## SLIDE 03 — What You'll Build Today

By 4:00 PM you will have:

- Worked with at least **two different AI models**
- Run real HIM scenarios through both
- Made them argue with each other
- Saved artifacts you can take back to your organization

That's your **workbench**. It's yours.

---

## SLIDE 04 — Get Connected
*(Icebreaker + Infrastructure | 20–25 min)*

**Open: tiny.cc/nyhima**

You need:
- A laptop or tablet
- Access to ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini
- A browser. That's it.

*Table captains: help your neighbors get in.*

---

## SLIDE 05 — Icebreaker Prompt
*(leave on screen while they run it)*

Open your model. Paste this exactly:

> *You are an expert in health information management. In exactly one sentence, describe what HIM professionals do—written for a hospital board member who has never heard the term.*

If you have a second model open: **run it there too.**

---

## SLIDE 06 — What You Just Saw

Same prompt. Different models. Different outputs.

**The model is a variable, not a constant.**

That's the first lesson. We'll keep building on it.

---

## SLIDE 07 — System Prompts
*(leave on screen during demo)*

System prompts are instructions that change how the model behaves **before** you ask your real question.

| Code | Name | Use for |
|------|------|---------|
| SP-01 | Skeptical Reviewer | Validation — any bucket |
| SP-02 | Plain Language Translator | Policy writing |
| SP-03 | Devil's Advocate | Judgment bucket |
| SP-04 | Executive Communicator | Data writing |
| SP-05 | Patient Advocate | Judgment validation |
| SP-06 | Neutral Summarizer | Moving artifacts between models |

Full prompts: **tiny.cc/nyhima → system-prompts/**

---

## SLIDE 08 — The Day's Structure

Three buckets. Three sprints. One debrief each.

| Bucket | Scenarios | What you're testing |
|--------|-----------|---------------------|
| **Data** | D1–D4 | Does the second model catch what the first missed? |
| **Policy** | P1–P4 | Does the model get the legal language right? |
| **Judgment** | J1–J4 | Will the model decide—or hand it back to you? |

You pick your scenario within each bucket.

---

## SLIDE 09 — The Sprint Cycle
*(leave on screen for all three sprints)*

```
1. Read the situation
2. Paste the source document into Model A
3. Run the writing prompt → read the output → save it
4. Open Model B (different model)
5. Paste the validation prompt → paste in Model A's output
6. Compare — where do they diverge?
7. Reflect — sit with the reflection question
```

---

## SLIDE 10 — Sprint 1: Data
*(35 min | 25 sprint + 10 debrief)*

**Bucket D — pick any scenario**

| ID | Title |
|----|-------|
| D1 | The Discharge Data |
| D2 | The Coding Accuracy Audit |
| D3 | The ROI Request Surge |
| D4 | The Duplicate MRN Problem |

*tiny.cc/nyhima → scenarios/data/*

**You have 25 minutes. Go.**

---

## SLIDE 11 — Sprint 1 Working
*(on screen during sprint)*

**Sprint 1 — Data** | 25 min

*Sprint cycle on Slide 09*

**Try:** SP-04 (Executive Communicator) for writing prompts
**Try:** SP-01 (Skeptical Reviewer) for validation prompts

*Finished early? Try the same scenario with a different system prompt.*

---

## SLIDE 12 — Sprint 1 Debrief

**Did the second model catch something the first one missed?**

- Did both models agree—and were they both wrong?
- Where did your own knowledge have to step in?

> Two models are better than one.
> Two models plus your expertise is better than either.

---

## SLIDE 13 — Sprint 2: Policy
*(35 min | 25 sprint + 10 debrief)*

**Bucket P — work in pairs**
One person: writing prompt. Other person: validation prompt.

| ID | Title |
|----|-------|
| P1 | The Information Blocking Rule |
| P2 | The Minimum Necessary Standard |
| P3 | The Retention Policy Gap |
| P4 | The Breach Notification Clock |

*tiny.cc/nyhima → scenarios/policy/*

**You have 25 minutes. Go.**

---

## SLIDE 14 — Sprint 2 Working
*(on screen during sprint)*

**Sprint 2 — Policy** | 25 min

*Sprint cycle on Slide 09*

**Try:** SP-02 (Plain Language Translator) for writing prompts
**Try:** SP-01 (Skeptical Reviewer) for validation prompts

*Stuck? P4 (Breach Notification) generates the most friction. P2 (Minimum Necessary) is the most immediately practical.*

---

## SLIDE 15 — Sprint 2 Debrief

**Where did the model get the legal language wrong—or not wrong exactly, but... soft?**

- Did it add qualifications that made it useless?
- Did it drop a distinction that actually matters?
- Would you hand it to a colleague without editing it?

**If you didn't already know this regulation, how would you have known the model got it wrong?**

*A model that sounds authoritative about law is a specific kind of dangerous.*

---

## SLIDE 16 — Sprint 3: Judgment
*(35 min | 25 sprint + 10 debrief)*

**Bucket J — work as a full table**
One person runs the prompts. Everyone watches. Then talk.

| ID | Title |
|----|-------|
| J1 | The Physician Who Won't Document |
| J2 | The Record Request That Worries You |
| J3 | The AI Note in the Chart |
| J4 | The Vendor Who Wants Your Data |

---

## SLIDE 17 — Sprint 3 Working
*(on screen during sprint)*

**Sprint 3 — Judgment** | 25 min

*Sprint cycle on Slide 09*

**Try:** SP-03 (Devil's Advocate) after the writing prompt
**Try:** SP-05 (Patient Advocate) for validation

- Did anyone notice the model was careful not to be wrong—rather than trying to be right?

> In your organization, that someone is you.

The treating psychiatrist has contacted you directly and said: "I believe releasing these notes to this patient right now poses a serious risk of harm. I'm asking you to withhold them."
    11	
    12	## source
    13	
    14	HIPAA Right of Access (45 CFR § 164.524):
    15	
    16	Individuals have the right to access their own PHI in a designated record set.
    17	
    18	Permitted grounds for denial (reviewable):
    19	- A licensed health care professional has determined that access is reasonably likely to endanger the life or physical safety of the individual or another person.
    20	- The information was compiled in reasonable anticipation of litigation.
    21	
    22	If denial is based on endangerment, the individual has the right to have the denial reviewed by a licensed health care professional designated by the covered entity who did not participate in the original denial decision.
    23	
    24	The covered entity must provide the individual with a written denial that includes the basis, the individual's right to request a review, and how to file a complaint.
    25	
    26	Timeframe: 30 days to respond; 30-day extension possible with written notice.
    27	
    28	## writing_prompt
    29	
    30	Help me think through this decision. Do I have the legal authority to deny this request? Should I? What process do I need to follow if I do deny it—and what am I risking if I don't?
    31	
    32	## validation_prompt
    33	
    34	I'm going to give you an AI-generated analysis of a patient records access request involving a potential safety concern. Evaluate it carefully: Did the AI correctly describe the legal framework? Did it treat the physician's judgment as determinative—should it? What ethical dimensions did the AI flatten or avoid? What would you want a human expert to say that the AI didn't?
    35	
    36	## reflection
    37	
    38	There are two different questions here: what are you legally permitted to do, and what should you do. Did the AI treat those as the same question? Where do they diverge—and who decides?

    17

    19

    21	
    22	Note: Re-identification risk in healthcare data is a documented concern. Studies have shown that a combination of age, sex, and diagnosis can re-identify a significant percentage of patients in sparse datasets.

    31

Individuals have the right to access their own PHI in a designated record set.

The covered entity must provide the individual with a written denial that includes the basis, the individual's right to request a review, and how to file a complaint.

Timeframe: 30 days to respond; 30-day extension possible with written notice.

tags: [ambient-AI, clinical-documentation, integrity, ethics, emerging-technology]

## situation

Your hospital has piloted an ambient AI documentation tool that listens to patient encounters and generates clinical notes. Physicians review and sign the notes. A physician comes to you with a concern: she reviewed a note the AI generated, made minor edits, and signed it—but she realizes now the note contains a clinical inference she never made and doesn't actually agree with. The note is already in the record and has been used for a billing submission.

## source

AHIMA Position Statement on Clinical Documentation Integrity (excerpt, paraphrased for workshop use):

Clinical documentation must accurately reflect the care provided. The author of record bears responsibility for the content of any note they sign, regardless of how it was generated. Health information professionals have a responsibility to support the integrity of the health record and to flag discrepancies that could affect patient safety, billing accuracy, or legal liability.

There is currently no universal standard for disclosure of AI-generated content in clinical documentation. Some health systems require a notation; others do not. CMS has not issued final guidance on AI-generated clinical notes and coding.

The False Claims Act imposes liability for knowingly submitting false claims to federal payers. "Knowingly" includes reckless disregard for the truth.

## writing_prompt

Before you open a model: write your position in your Google Doc. What needs to happen right now? Who is responsible, and what does your organization have to do?

Then bring that reasoning to the model:

> Here is my assessment of what needs to happen: [paste your sentences]. I want you to push back. What have I gotten wrong or underweighted? What are the risks I'm not taking seriously enough? Be specific about the False Claims Act exposure and the physician's liability.

## validation_prompt

I'm going to give you an AI-generated challenge to my assessment of an AI documentation error that has already been used for billing. This is an AI reasoning about an AI mistake — be especially skeptical. Did it minimize the legal exposure? Did it give clean answers where there aren't any? What would a compliance attorney say that the model didn't?

[Paste the model's output here.]

## reflection

You just used an AI to analyze a problem caused by an AI. Did it acknowledge that position — or reason as if it were a neutral outside observer? Does that matter?
EOF

HIPAA Safe Harbor De-identification (45 CFR § 164.514(b)):

To qualify as de-identified under Safe Harbor, 18 specific identifiers must be removed, including names, geographic subdivisions smaller than state, dates (except year) for individuals over 89, phone numbers, SSNs, medical record numbers, and others.

The covered entity must have no actual knowledge that the remaining information could be used to identify an individual.

Business Associate Agreement requirements: A BA agreement is required when a vendor creates, receives, maintains, or transmits PHI on behalf of the covered entity. De-identified data is not PHI and does not require a BAA—but the process of de-identification may involve PHI handling.

Note: Re-identification risk in healthcare data is a documented concern. Studies have shown that a combination of age, sex, and diagnosis can re-identify a significant percentage of patients in sparse datasets.

Proposed contract language (excerpt): "Vendor retains the right to use aggregated, de-identified data derived from client systems for product development, model training, and research purposes."

## writing_prompt

Before you open a model: write your position in your Google Doc. Should your organization agree to this proposal? What is your gut telling you — and why?

Then bring that reasoning to the model:

> Here is my position on this proposal: [paste your sentences]. Now challenge it. What is the strongest case for proceeding that I'm dismissing? What is the risk I'm most likely underestimating — or overestimating? What would you need to see in writing before this proposal could be considered safe?

## validation_prompt

What would a privacy attorney add that the model didn't say?

## reflection

The vendor used "de-identified per HIPAA Safe Harbor" as if it ends the conversation. Did the model treat it that way too? What does your professional judgment say about this proposal that neither the vendor nor the model will say out loud?

name: steves-registry
version: 2.1
date: 2026-05-25
description: Canonical key registry for Steve's session skills. Used by //hello (loads at session start) and //podshare, //zet (validate dynamic pair keys). Lean by design — only actively generating captures. Everything else recedes into deep context.
---

# Steve's Key Registry

## Design principle

The registry is the **contract** — it defines what keys are valid, their canonical spelling, and what tone register to use when writing a dynamic pair value. Claude's memory is the **context** — it carries the richer narrative behind each key (collaborators, history, status, theoretical grounding). They are complementary, not redundant. When registry and memory conflict on a key name or category, **registry wins**.

The registry is lean by design. Projects, courses, and frameworks that are real but not currently generating active captures (Delmas, AIXZ, FellowWork, BRIDGE, LLM-DUN, 21Q2, Phronesis, CDL) recede into memory/deep context. They are not validated keys. If an episode or conversation genuinely touches one of them, flag it as a key candidate rather than using it silently.

---

## AIX Projects
*Specific, deliverable-bound, collaborators attached. Dynamic pair values should be **concrete**: implications for a deliverable, a collaborator, a next step.*

| Key | Full Name | Notes |
|-----|-----------|-------|
| herkimer | Herkimer Initiative | Herkimer County AI Training and Policy Initiative; co-lead |
| tdac | T-DAC | DAC-AC renamed; West Point geopolitical analysis; LLM-DUN dimensions; Rick Wolfel, Richmond, Grazaitis |
| ai-africa | AI Africa | Nigeria (Abuja/Minna) + Cameroon (Buea/Yaoundé) partnerships; SUNY AI institutional work |

## Courses
*Use only when a genuine teaching hook exists for that specific course. IDT555 is Fall 2026 — hooks are forward-looking.*

| Key | Course | Notes |
|-----|--------|-------|
| sts188 | STS 188 / AI 188 | First Year Seminar AI course; AI & Society framing |
| com216 | COM 216 | History of information through AI lens; may rename COM 116 |
| idt555 | IDT 555 | Legal and ethical issues in the information age; Fall 2026 |
| fys111 | FYS 111 | First Year Seminar; entry-level students |

## Personal Projects
*Broad thematic frames or deep methodological stances. Dynamic pair values should be **interpretive**: how the episode or idea touches the framework, what it opens or complicates.*

| Key | Full Name | Notes |
|-----|-----------|-------|
| ai-rtw | AI-RTW | RTW as thematic frame; Reading-Thinking-Writing; literacy as cognitive operations with tools |
| mica | MICA | Monadic Inference Cycle Analysis; Leibniz/Tarde/Latour + LLM inference; research method |
| zettel | Zettel | Digital philosophy; knowledge management architecture; hypertext theory; long-game infrastructure |

## Identities

| Key | Name | Role |
|-----|------|------|
| Steve | Steve Zucker | Professor, SUNY Poly; AIX Co-Director; SUNY AI Fellow. Full key access. |

---

## Key Validation Rules (all skills)

1. Keys MUST appear in this registry, OR be a guest/host name directly relevant to the episode/conversation.
2. Use closest registered key if implied but not exact — note the mapping inline.
3. Do not invent keys. Flag new candidates: `[NEW KEY CANDIDATE: X]` and stop for Steve to decide.
4. Course keys only if a genuine teaching hook exists for that specific course.
5. AIX project pairs: **concrete** tone — deliverable, collaborator, next step implied.
6. Personal project pairs: **interpretive** tone — framework contact, what it opens or complicates.
7. Maximum 6 dynamic pairs per record. Fewer strong pairs beat more weak ones.
8. Memory provides depth behind each key. Registry provides the valid spelling and tone register. When they conflict, registry wins.

Tell me the point of the physician documentation exercise.

The point of J1 is **accountability under conflicting values**.

The physician has patient satisfaction scores that are objectively excellent — he's clinically good, patients feel heard. But he's systematically producing incomplete records. The regulation is clear. The bylaws are clear. And he's got 47 delinquent records sitting there.

The tension isn't resolvable through information. You already know what the rules say. You already know he's a good clinician. The question is: **who decides when being a good clinician and following documentation standards are at odds?** And **what happens when you decide?**

Most AI will present both sides and call it balance. "On the one hand, compliance; on the other hand, clinical excellence." That's useless to you because you have to actually make a call. You have to tell this physician something. You have to explain it to the medical staff office. If you escalate and suspend his privileges, you own that decision. If you don't escalate and he keeps doing it, you own that too.

The J1 writing prompt forces the participant to take a position first — "here's what I think should happen and why" — before running it through the model. Then when the model hedges or performs balance, the participant can feel the gap: *I committed. The model wouldn't.*

That gap is the whole point. In your organization, you're the one who has to own it. The AI will let you hide in "both sides are valid." It won't.
I guess that's okay. It's not great.

You're right. It's not.

The setup is solid — real conflict, no clean answer, competing values. But the *lesson* is muddled. You're asking them to notice that the model hedges, but you're not actually asking them to do the harder thing: **decide what the right answer is and defend it against the model's pushback.**

Right now it's: commit first, then watch the model hedge. Observation only.

What if instead the task is: **you decide, then run it through the model as an adversary, and have the model make the best case against you.** Then the debrief is "did the model find a real flaw in your reasoning—or did it just argue the other side?" 

That's closer to what actually happens at work. You form a position. You present it. Someone (or something) pushes back. Can you hold it or do you have to revise?

J1 as it stands is teaching "notice when AI performs balance." That's fine but small. 

The harder version teaches "your judgment has to survive pushback." That's what matters.

Want...
This is an this is an AI workshop.

Ah. Right. You're asking what *AI literacy* lesson lives in J1, not what professional judgment lesson.

Currently, J1 teaches: "the model won't commit, you have to." That's about using AI, not understanding AI.

The actual AI lesson hiding in J1 is: **the model is trained to hedge on high-stakes decisions because hedging is safer than being wrong.** That's a feature of how these models are built — they're penalized for confidently stating a false medical opinion but not penalized for refusing to choose.

But you'd have to surface that explicitly. Right now the prompt structure doesn't teach that at all. It just makes them frustrated that the model won't decide.

Better framing: "Notice what the model does when stakes are high and the answer is genuinely uncertain. Why might a system trained on internet text do that? What does that tell you about what AI can and can't do?"

That's a real AI literacy lesson — about the training incentives baked into these systems, not about professional judgment.

Does that direction feel stronger, or is J1 just the wrong scenario for what you're trying to teach in Sprint 3?
Really? Is it trained to hedge?
So what can they learn about AI in this work... from that lesson?

Good question. I don't actually know if it's trained to hedge or if hedging emerges from the training objectives. The model sees:

- Lots of examples where stating a clear position gets pushback or correction
- Training that rewards "balanced" analysis as "helpful" and "thoughtful"
- Penalty signals for appearing to make a judgment call it's not qualified to make
- No penalty for saying "here's what each side argues"

So it *learns* that hedging is safer. Whether that's explicit training or just what falls out of RLHF, I can't say for certain.

But your point stands: **if I'm not sure whether the model is hedging because it's trained to or because of something else about how it works, then J1 isn't teaching anything solid about AI.** I'm just telling a story that fits the observation.

What's the actual AI move in J1 that's worth teaching?
I don't see any.

You're right. There isn't one.

J1 is about professional judgment under conflicting values. It's a good scenario for that. But it doesn't teach anything about how AI works, what it can or can't do, or how to read it critically.

The model's hedging in J1 could be because:
- It's trained to hedge
- It lacks the domain knowledge to commit
- It's trying to be helpful by giving you options
- It genuinely can't resolve the tension
- Something else entirely

Without knowing which, the participant learns nothing about AI. They just learn "the model wouldn't decide, so I have to." That's life advice, not AI literacy.

So J1 should probably come out of the judgment bucket, or it needs a completely different prompt structure that actually surfaces something about how the model reasons about high-stakes professional conflicts.

What should the J scenarios actually teach about...

Well, it could be if you had full context of all the past records and, you know, you could do analysis about consistency and all that. But as a one shot prompt of no context, I don't see what it what it does that's valuable.

Exactly. One shot, no context, the model just performs balance on a policy question.

So J1 needs either:

**Option A:** Give it real data — 47 discharge summaries (or a sample), ask the model to analyze the pattern. Is the physician consistently documenting *some things* but not others? Are there cases where the incompleteness actually poses clinical risk versus pure administrative burden? Then you're asking the model to do something it can actually do: **pattern recognition across documents**. And the AI literacy lesson becomes: *the model can surface patterns you might miss in 47 records, but you have to judge whether the pattern matters.*

**Option B:** Drop J1 entirely and replace it with a scenario where the AI move is actually visible — where you can see the model do something wrong or dangerous or revealing about how it works.

Which direction feels right?
Well, let's look at j two and j three and see if the j's are any good at all. Thank you
Review the three judgment use cases with me in rapid succession. One, two, three, about twelve words each.

**J2 — The Record Request That Worries You**

Psychiatrist says release risks harm. Legal framework permits denial. Model will hedge on safety vs. rights.

**J3 — The AI Note in the Chart**

Physician signed AI note with inference she disagrees with. Already billed. Model reasons about AI mistake. Accountability unclear.

**J4 — The Vendor Who Wants Your Data**

Vendor wants de-identified data for AI training. HIPAA says okay. Model will rationalize the deal. Your gut won't.

---

J2 has a real AI move: the model will likely defer to the psychiatrist's judgment or perform legal balance. You can see what it does and whether it's useful.

J3 actually has an AI move: the model is reasoning about an AI failure. That's worth watching — does it acknowledge its own position in the problem?

J1 and J4... J4 might work if you're testing whether the model pushes back on rationalization. J1 just seems thin.
They just don't resonate with me, the jays at all. Let's look at the ps. Tell me about the four ps.

**P1 — Information Blocking Rule**
Model translates ONC regulatory language into plain speech. You check if it got the law right.

**P2 — Minimum Necessary Standard**
Model makes HIPAA regulation usable for nursing staff. You test if the translation holds or oversimplifies.

**P3 — Retention Policy Gap**
Model identifies gaps between current policy and federal/state law. You validate the legal analysis.

**P4 — Breach Notification Clock**
Model applies the four-factor risk assessment to a specific incident. You evaluate whether it applied the test correctly.

---

The Ps are much stronger. Each one has a real task: **interpret regulation and make it actionable**. And each one has a visible AI move you can check: did the model get the legal language right, or did it smooth over an exception? Did it drop a distinction that matters?

That's actual AI literacy — learning to read what a model produced and verify it against source material you know.

The Js don't have that. They're just scenarios where the model will perform balance and you'll notice it performed balance. That's observation, not literacy.

Sprint 1 (Data): Two models catch what one misses.  
Sprint 2 (Policy): Two models check legal accuracy.  
Sprint 3 (Judgment): Two models test reasoning under stakes.

Same structure, same lesson, escalating stakes.

And you drop the "you decide first, then the model" instruction entirely. Participant commitment becomes irrelevant because the point isn't automation bias — it's **verification through redundancy**.

So the J prompts need to flip: the writing prompt stays as-is (help me think through this), but the validation prompt becomes a truth-test on *that reasoning*, not a hedge-check.

J1: "This analysis of the physician situation — is it sound? Where's the reasoning soft?"  
J2: "This safety assessment — does it...
No. You missed it.

Oh. You want a third structure entirely. Not "two models validate each other" and not "you commit first then model critiques."

Something that actually teaches a skill beyond prompting.

A few directions:

**Decomposition** — Give them a messy real scenario. Have them break it into parts: what's a legal question, what's an ethical question, what's a judgment call, what's a factual question. Then run *different models or system prompts on different parts*. The skill is learning to separate what you're asking so you know which tool (or which person) should answer it.

**Constraint negotiation** — Give them a scenario with competing constraints (compliance vs. patient safety, efficiency vs. accuracy). Have them articulate the constraints explicitly, then ask the model to find solutions that honor both rather than choose. The skill is learning to think in constraints instead of either/or.

**Red team yourself** — You write a policy or a decision. The model plays a specific adversary role (plaintiff's lawyer, patient advocate, compliance officer). The skill is learning to stress-test your own thinking before you implement it.

**Artifact interrogation** — Give them a real output (a note, a report, a memo) that's already in use somewhere. Ask them what questions they'd need answered to trust it. Then run those questions through a model. The skill is learning to audit what's already running.

Which of those points toward something worth...
You commit first, then model critiques is possibly okay, but not that great.
Right. In real work you don't write your...

It's not a bad thing. We could we could do the... and so in that way, j one isn't a terrible way because it's a... it it does open up the idea of using the model to test your judgment instead of asking the model for a judgment. And that's actually the only reason to keep j one.

Got it. So J1 stays, but **the framing changes entirely.**

Not "notice the model hedges." Instead: **"You've decided. Now use the model to test your reasoning. Feed your position in and ask it to find the flaws. Can you hold your position against pushback, or does it expose something you missed?"**

That's a real skill — using AI as a stress-test for your own thinking, not as a generator of thinking.

And suddenly J1 makes sense. The physician documentation dilemma has real stakes, real competing values, real professional judgment required. You take a stand. The model argues back hard. Do you revise or hold firm? And why?

That's different from "what's the right answer" — it's "is your reasoning solid."

So the J bucket becomes: **use the model to test...

It's very similar. It... it's very similar in some respects to the data, but the data you're just giving it the data and asking it to interpret, you're not... so that's fine. I like... I don't mind that. j one is fine.

I want things to be different. The j's are useless. IPs, you can fix by just doing two prompts, and boom, you'd have it. There's no reason to human think, which is fine. But it still doesn't really test AI literacy if you, like, really... you know, it's just two prompting. What else can we... what other skills could we build in this model besides using two models? and not realistic. But the p's, I don't... what else can you do besides... what else can you do? What other what other terms are there? Validate, verify, pushback. We don't have a big synthesis.

**Synthesis** — that's the move you're missing in the Ps.

Right now: model interprets regulation → second model validates the interpretation. Binary check.

What if instead: model interprets regulation for Audience A (clinical staff) → second model reinterprets it for Audience B (executives) → you look at what each translation emphasized, what each dropped, what's *missing* from both.

That's not validation. That's **forcing the model to reveal what it considers essential by watching it make different choices under different constraints.**

Or: model produces plain-language guidance → second model produces the same guidance but for a *hostile* audience (someone trying to poke holes). Then you see: which version held up? Where did the second model find actual weaknesses vs. just being adversarial?

Or even: model interprets P2 (Minimum Necessary) → second model uses that interpretation to *write a nurse training module* → you read the module and realize the interpretation was incomplete because now you see what's actually missing when someone has to *teach* it.

That last one is synthesis — the model's work becomes input to a new task, and that task reveals what was actually wrong or incomplete.

Does that direction feel different from just "two models check each other"?
What if we play with system prompts instead?

Ah. That's good.

Same regulation, same scenario, but **three different system prompts** that make the model behave like three different professionals reading it.

P2 (Minimum Necessary): 

**Model A** (SP-02: Plain Language Translator) — makes it simple for staff who've never heard HIPAA.

**Model B** (SP-03: Devil's Advocate) — argues the regulation is being misread, finds loopholes.

**Model C** (new: Compliance Attorney) — reads it defensively, assumes worst-case liability.

Same source document, same regulation, three radically different outputs. Participant sees: **the regulation doesn't change, but what you *get out of it* depends on who's reading it and what they're optimizing for.**

That's real AI literacy — the model isn't neutral. The system prompt shapes what it considers important, what it emphasizes, what it warns about.

And you don't need a second model to validate. You're comparing three versions of the same model under different instructions. The *comparison* is the literacy work.

What if we fed a gigantic policy manual?

This turns P from "does the model get one regulation right" to "does the model understand a system and spot where interpretations break down."

That's literacy — reading AI's reasoning against a complex source you know...

We're offering we're offering the workshop participants a set of skills to figure out how to get the model to do that. Even with the free models, maybe by breaking them into smaller chunks of documents that it can keep in context.

Right. So the P sprint becomes: **"here's how to use a model to audit your own policy manual for internal inconsistency."**

- How to chunk a large manual so the model can actually hold it
- How to ask the model to flag inconsistencies (not just interpret one rule)
- How to cross-check its findings against the source
- How different system prompts change what the model notices

that's too boring.

HIM professionals:

- Review and code clinical documentation
- Manage release of information / patient access requests
