    89	### Visual inspection (rasterize pages)
    90	
    91	Text extraction is **blind** to charts, diagrams, figures, equations,
    92	multi-column layout, and form structures. When any of these matter,
    93	rasterize the relevant page and Read the image:
    94	
    95	```bash
    96	# Rasterize a single page (page 3 here) at 150 DPI
    97	pdftoppm -jpeg -r 150 -f 3 -l 3 document.pdf /tmp/page
    98	
    99	# pdftoppm zero-pads the output filename based on TOTAL page count
   100	# (e.g., page-03.jpg for a 50-page PDF, page-003.jpg for 200+ pages)
   101	# Don't guess the filename — find it:
   102	ls /tmp/page-*.jpg
   103	```
   104	
   105	Then Read the resulting image file. This gives you full visual
   106	understanding of that page — layout, charts, equations, everything.
   107	
   108	**When to rasterize vs. text-extract:**
   109	- **Content/data questions → text extraction** (cheaper, searchable)
   110	- **Figures, charts, visual layout → rasterize the page**
   111	- **Tables → try text extraction first, rasterize if garbled**
   112	- **Precision matters → do both** (extract text AND rasterize; use text
   113	  for data, image for context — this is what Claude's API does natively
   114	  with PDF uploads)
   115	
   116	**Token cost awareness:**
   117	- Text extraction: ~200–400 tokens per page
   118	- Rasterized image: ~1,600 tokens per page (at 150 DPI)
   119	- Both together: ~2,000–2,400 tokens per page
   120	
   121	For a 100-page PDF, rasterizing everything would consume ~160K tokens.
   122	Only rasterize pages that matter for the question at hand.
   123	
   124	### Choosing your reading strategy
   125	
   126	**Text-heavy documents** (reports, articles, books):
   127	→ Text extraction is primary. Rasterize only for specific figures or
   128	  pages where layout matters.
   129	
   130	**Scanned documents** (`pdffonts` shows no fonts):
   131	→ `pdftotext` will return nothing — don't run it. Rasterize pages at
   132	  150 DPI and Read them visually. For bulk text extraction, use OCR
   133	  (pytesseract after converting pages to images — see REFERENCE.md for
   134	  a complete example).
   135	
   136	**Slide-deck PDFs** (exported presentations):
   137	→ Every page is primarily visual. Rasterize individual pages on demand.
   138	  Text extraction gives you bullet-point text but loses all layout.
   139	
   140	**Form-heavy documents**:
   141	→ Extract form field values programmatically first (see below). Rasterize
   142	  the form page for visual context if needed.
   143	
   144	**Data-heavy documents** (tables, charts, figures):
   145	→ Use pdfplumber for tables. Rasterize pages with charts/figures.
   146	  Extract text for surrounding narrative. Consider both text AND image
   147	  for the same page when precision matters.
   148	
   149	### Extracting embedded images
   150	
   151	```bash
   152	# List all embedded images with metadata (size, color, compression)
   153	pdfimages -list document.pdf
   154	
   155	# Extract all images as PNG
   156	pdfimages -png document.pdf /tmp/img
   157	
   158	# Extract from specific pages only (pages 3-5)
   159	pdfimages -png -f 3 -l 5 document.pdf /tmp/img
   160	
   161	# Extract in original format (JPEG stays JPEG, etc.)
   162	pdfimages -all document.pdf /tmp/img
   163	```
   164	
   165	Then Read `/tmp/img-000.png` (etc.) to see each extracted image.
   166	
   167	**Gotcha — vector graphics:** `pdfimages` extracts only raster image
   168	data. Charts and diagrams drawn as vector graphics (common in
   169	matplotlib, Excel, and R exports) will NOT appear — they are page
   170	content operators, not image objects. For these, rasterize the whole
   171	page with `pdftoppm` instead.
   172	
   173	**Gotcha — empty images:** `pdfimages` sometimes produces many tiny or
   174	empty image files — these are typically background masks, transparency
   175	layers, or decorative elements. Filter by file size to find the real
   176	content images.
   177	
   178	Programmatic extraction with position data:
   179	```python
   180	import fitz  # PyMuPDF
   181	
   182	doc = fitz.open("document.pdf")
   183	for page in doc:
   184	    for img in page.get_images():
   185	        xref = img[0]
   186	        pix = fitz.Pixmap(doc, xref)
   187	        if pix.n - pix.alpha > 3:  # CMYK or other non-RGB
   188	            pix = fitz.Pixmap(fitz.csRGB, pix)
   189	        pix.save(f"/tmp/img_{xref}.png")
   190	```
   191	
   192	### Extracting file attachments
   193	
   194	PDFs can contain embedded files — spreadsheets, data files, other
   195	documents. Common in business reports, PDF portfolios, and PDF/A-3
   196	compliance documents.
   197	
   198	```bash
   199	# List all attachments
   200	pdfdetach -list document.pdf
   201	
   202	# Extract all attachments to a directory
   203	mkdir -p /tmp/attachments
   204	pdfdetach -saveall -o /tmp/attachments/ document.pdf
   205	
   206	# Extract a specific attachment by number (1-based index from -list output)
   207	pdfdetach -save 1 -o /tmp/attachment.pdf document.pdf
   208	```
   209	
   210	In Python:
   211	```python
   212	import os
   213	from pypdf import PdfReader
   214	
   215	reader = PdfReader("document.pdf")
   216	for name, content_list in reader.attachments.items():
   217	    safe_name = os.path.basename(name)  # sanitize — name comes from the PDF
   218	    for content in content_list:
   219	        with open(f"/tmp/{safe_name}", "wb") as f:
   220	            f.write(content)
   221	```
   222	
   223	**Two attachment mechanisms exist in PDFs:** page-level file annotation
   224	attachments (shown as paperclip icons in viewers) and document-level
   225	embedded files (in the EmbeddedFiles name tree). Both `pdfdetach` and
   226	pypdf handle the common cases. Rich media assets (3D, video) embedded
   227	as annotations may not appear in the attachment list — use PyMuPDF to
   228	iterate page annotations for those.
   229	
   230	### Extracting form field data
   231	
   232	PDFs with interactive forms (government forms, applications, contracts)
   233	have fillable fields whose values can be read programmatically:
   234	
   235	```python
   236	from pypdf import PdfReader
   237	
   238	reader = PdfReader("form.pdf")
   239	
   240	# Text input fields only:
   241	fields = reader.get_form_text_fields()
   242	for name, value in fields.items():
   243	    print(f"{name}: {value}")
   244	
   245	# All field types (checkboxes, radio buttons, dropdowns too):
   246	all_fields = reader.get_fields() or {}
   247	for name, field in all_fields.items():
   248	    print(f"{name}: {field.get('/V', '')} (type: {field.get('/FT', '')})")
   249	```
   250	
   251	`get_form_text_fields()` returns only text input fields. For
   252	government forms and contracts that use checkboxes, radio buttons,
   253	and dropdowns, use `get_fields()` instead to see all field types.
   254	
   255	For comprehensive field info (types, options, defaults):
   256	```bash
   257	pdftk form.pdf dump_data_fields
   258	```
   259	
   260	For anything beyond reading form data — filling forms, creating forms —
   261	use the pdf skill at `/mnt/skills/public/pdf/SKILL.md`.
   262	
   263	### Audio, video, and other rare embedded content
   264	
   265	PDFs can occasionally embed audio, video, or 3D models. Check
   266	`pdfdetach -list` first — if the media appears as an attachment,
   267	extract with `pdfdetach -saveall`. If not, it may be a Rich Media
   268	annotation (harder to extract; requires PyMuPDF to iterate page
   269	annotations). This is very rare in practice. Most PDF viewers outside
   270	Adobe Acrobat do not support media playback.
   271	
   272	### Font diagnostics
   273	
   274	If text extraction produces garbled output (wrong characters, missing
   275	text, mojibake), look back at the `pdffonts` output from the Content
   276	inventory. Check the "emb" column — fonts showing "no" (not embedded)
   277	with custom encodings mean the PDF's character mapping may be broken
   278	for text extraction. In that case, rasterize the page and use vision
   279	instead.
   280	
   281	Also check encoding: fonts with "Custom" or "Identity-H" encoding
   282	without embedded CIDToGID maps can cause character substitution issues
   283	even when the font is technically embedded.
   284	
   285	---
   286	
   287	## Quick Reference
   288	
   289	| Task | Best Tool | Command/Code |
   290	|------|-----------|--------------|
   291	| Inspect PDF | poppler-utils | `pdfinfo`, `pdfimages -list`, `pdfdetach -list`, `pdffonts` |
   292	| Extract text | pdfplumber | `page.extract_text()` |
   293	| Extract text (CLI) | pdftotext | `pdftotext -layout input.pdf output.txt` |
   294	| Extract tables | pdfplumber | `page.extract_tables()` |
   295	| See page visually | pdftoppm | `pdftoppm -jpeg -r 150 -f N -l N` |
   296	| Extract images | pdfimages | `pdfimages -png input.pdf prefix` |
   297	| Extract attachments | pdfdetach | `pdfdetach -saveall -o /tmp/` |
   298	| Read form fields | pypdf | `reader.get_fields()` |
   299	| OCR scanned PDFs | pytesseract | Convert to image first |
   300	
   301	## PDF Form Filling, Creation, Merging, Splitting, and Other Operations
   302	
   303	This skill covers **reading and inspection** only. For filling forms,
   304	creating, merging, splitting, rotating, watermarking, encrypting, or
   305	other PDF manipulation tasks, use the public pdf skill at
   306	`/mnt/skills/public/pdf/SKILL.md`.
   307

 Introduction
Care Compare on Medicare.gov is a consumer-oriented website that provides information on the quality-of-care hospitals are providing
to their patients. This information can help consumers make informed decisions about health care. Care Compare on Medicare.gov
allows consumers to select up to three hospitals and directly compare performance measure information related to heart attack,
emergency department care, preventive care, and other conditions. The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) created the
website to better inform health care consumers about a hospital’s quality of care. CMS provides data on over 4,000 Medicare-certified
hospitals, including acute care hospitals, critical access hospitals (CAHs), children’s hospitals, Veterans Health Administration (VHA)
Medical Centers, Department of Defense (DoD) and hospital outpatient departments. Care Compare on Medicare.gov is part of an
Administration-wide effort to increase the availability and accessibility of information on quality, utilization, and costs for effective,
informed decision-making. More information about hospital public reporting can be found by visiting the CMS.gov website and
performing a search for Hospital Quality Initiative Public Reporting. To access the Care Compare on Medicare.gov website, please visit
Medicare.gov/care-compare.

Hospital Quality Initiative Public Reporting websites are typically updated, or refreshed, each quarter in January, April, July, and
October; however, the refresh schedule is subject to change and not all measures will update during each quarterly release.

See the Measure Descriptions and Reporting Cycles section of this Data Dictionary for additional information. Hospital data are reported
in median time only; however, the median time is often referred to as the “average time” to allow for ease of understanding across a
wider audience.

Links to download the data from the individual datasets in comma-separated value (CSV) flat file format can be found on the Provider
Data Catalog (PDC) on Medicare.gov site with each dataset. To view the Announcements, About the data information, and a link to the
data archives, go to the Topics page.

All Hospital Quality Initiative Public Reporting websites are publicly accessible. As works of the U.S. government, public reporting
data are in the public domain and permission is not required to reuse them. An attribution to the agency as the source is appreciated.
Your materials, however, should not give the false impression of government endorsement of your commercial products or services.


Document Purpose
The purpose of this document is to provide a directory of material for use in the navigation of information contained within the
Provider Data Catalog (PDC) downloadable databases. The Appendix A – Hospital Quality Initiatives Public Reporting Measures
section in this data dictionary provides a full list of measures contained in the downloadable databases. The Measure Dates section of
this data dictionary provides additional information about measure dates and quarters.

The following Specification Manuals are available on Qualitynet.cms.gov:
    • Specifications Manual for Hospital Inpatient Quality (IQR) Measures
    • Hospital Outpatient Quality Reporting (OQR) Specifications Manual
    • Ambulatory Surgical Center Quality Reporting Specifications Manual
    • Specification Resources for IPFQR Program Measures
    • PCHQR Program Manual

The prompt for Model B could be as simple as:

**Argument for same model, fresh conversation:**

A fresh conversation has no memory of the previous work. The model reads your artifact cold, without the context of how you made it. That's actually closer to how a real colleague reads your memo — they don't know your process, they just see the output.

Same model might have the same systematic biases in both conversations. If it missed something in Round 2, it might miss it again in Round 3. A truly different model (Claude or ChatGPT) would catch what Gemini overlooked.

Or even simpler with error handling:

```bash
#!/bin/bash

REPO="${2:-.}"
MSG="$1"

cd "$REPO" || exit 1
git pull || exit 1
git add . || exit 1
git commit -m "$MSG" || exit 1
git push || exit 1
```

Each `|| exit 1` stops the chain if anything fails. Safer than `&&` alone because it tells you exactly where it broke.

But access only matters if it comes with understanding: what AI actually is, what it can and cannot do, ethical implications for healthcare, data, people.

For HIM professionals: treat AI literacy as a workplace expectation — supported through continuing education, embedded in professional standards, considered in hiring and advancement decisions.

That's the frame. You said critical review identified: sharper directive AI definition (accepted), sequencing of framing (accepted), rhetorical provocation "AI prompts you" (retained), invisibility as dimension (retained).

What do you want to do with it?
There's a couple of things we need to address.
What are they?
Many of their systems are directive.

Right. So the talk needs to name that directly — not theoretically, but with concrete examples from HIM work.

**What systems are already directive in their workflows?**

- EHR clinical decision support flags
- Coding suggestion tools
- Breach risk flagging
- Duplicate record alerts
- Documentation completeness warnings
- Revenue cycle recommendations

These aren't prompts. The AI surfaces a recommendation *before* the professional has formed their own judgment. That's directive.

The talk should probably open or anchor on that reality: "The AI you already use isn't the kind you ask questions. It's the kind that tells you what to do."

Then: "Today we're going to work with the kind you ask — because understanding how to use that intentionally makes you better at reading the directive kind that's already in your workflows."

Does that address it, or is there more to the directive AI problem in HIM systems that needs...

So the literacy the literacy that I discussed, reading, thinking, writing is purely compositional, but I wanna make a case that it's important to understand and to have experienced the compositional in order to provide leadership and training in the directive. It's not necessary to be fully versed in the compositional if you're going to only be using the directive. I

So the argument reframes:

**You don't need compositional literacy to *use* directive AI.** You need it to **lead and train** people who are using it, or to **audit and govern** it in your organization.

That's different. And it's stronger for an HIM audience because many of them will never prompt a model — they'll only see recommendations surfaced in their EHR or coding system.

But **if you're designing policies around AI, training staff on it, deciding whether to deploy it, auditing its outputs** — then you need to have *experienced* what the model can and can't do in a compositional context. Otherwise you're flying blind on governance.

Does that reframe feel right? And does that change what the talk should say about who this literacy is *for*?

Unless they wanna get a promotion and be leadership. If they wanna get a master's degree in health information management. In fact, I think if they wanna get a bachelor's degree in health information management, they need to be literate in the reading, thinking, and writing with AI. Not if they wanna be a coder, but if they wanna supervise coders. And maybe I don't understand what coders do or if they have degrees or not, but I just imagine that there's associate's degree level work that's directive and bachelor's level work may be directive, but supervisory level work would require compositional litters.

That's the real argument.

**Compositional AI literacy is a credential requirement for HIM leadership and education, not for individual contributors.**

- **Associate degree / individual contributor:** You use directive AI (coding suggestions, record flags, workflow recommendations). You don't need to prompt models.

- **Bachelor's degree / supervisory level:** You need to understand compositional AI so you can audit, govern, and train people using directive AI. You need to have felt what the model can and can't do.

- **Master's degree / organizational leadership:** You absolutely need compositional literacy. You're making institutional decisions about which AI systems to deploy, how to govern them, what policies to write.

That's a **credential-leveled literacy framework**. And it's much stronger than "everyone should have AI literacy." It's **"if you want to lead in HIM, you must have compositional AI literacy."**

The talk should say: *Here's what you need to know if you're going to supervise people using AI. Here's what you need to have experienced. And here's why the three hours we're doing today — reading, thinking, writing — is actually professional development for future leaders.*

Does that land right?

So the talk, the three hours we did yesterday in the workshop was professional development for future leaders because it was compositional. And that's why we didn't focus on... so I will use the same intro, but this talk is the case for why the compositional is critically important.

Yes. Um, but directive is like... we'll have to look at the use cases. We didn't do any use cases for Nyhemiah. But are there some use cases... go back. **J1:** Physician documentation deficiency — the system flags incomplete records before you see them.

**J2:** Patient access safety concern — the system surfaces a potential harm risk.

**J4:** Vendor data proposal — the system recommends whether to proceed.

The workshop was **"experience the compositional so you can lead the directive."**

The talk is **"here's why that matters in your actual work."**

---

So the DPJ against RTW,

ok, let's work on the p, the policy. i have these use cases, but i think e decided was to go with real data, policy documents. let them choose from a curated set?

Yes. That's what the Round 2 document library is. Seven documents, they pick one, work through it with two models.

What's the question — are the seven documents the right ones, or are you rethinking what "curated set" means?
where are they?

They're not built yet. They're in the Cowork task as a to-do list. The old P scenarios (P1-P4) exist but they're in the old sprint structure — they need to be rewritten for the Round 2 read-think-write format.

What exists right now in outputs:
- P1-P4 in the original scenario format (writing prompt / validation prompt / reflection)
- R2 versions of some of them already built in the B1 cowork folder (from an earlier session) — information blocking, minimum necessary, breach notification, vendor BAA, Joint Commission RC, CMS CoP, ROI policy

Those R2 versions are close but were built before the workshop was redesigned. They use the old two-model validation structure, not the read-think-write + workbench prompt structure.

Do you want to:

**A:** Pull up the existing R2 documents and revise them to fit the new structure

**B:** Start fresh with the new structure and build them cleanly

**C:** Look at one of the existing R2 documents together and decide if it needs much work
no, the document need to be discovered. i need an open source repo of these kind of dox

Right. You need a source — a place where real policy documents, regulations, and standards live publicly so participants can find and use them, not just get handed an excerpt.

The good news: most of what you need is already public domain.

**Federal regulations — free, authoritative:**
- `ecfr.gov` — Electronic Code of Federal Regulations. HIPAA, CMS CoP, ONC rules all live here. Full text, searchable, linkable to specific sections.
- `hhs.gov` — HHS publishes HIPAA guidance, breach notification rules, minimum necessary standards as plain-language documents alongside the regulatory text.
- `cms.gov` — Conditions of Participation, hospital quality standards, coding guidelines.

**Standards bodies — some free, some not:**
- Joint Commission standards — unfortunately paywalled for most content.
- AHIMA — some guidance free, most member-gated.

**Contracts and BAAs — tricky:**
No public repo of real vendor BAAs exists. You'd have to write fictional examples or use templates from AHIMA or HHS model BAA language (which is public).

**The design question:** Do you want participants to go find their own document from one of these sources, or do you curate a short list of direct links — "here are seven specific URLs, pick one, upload it"?

Direct links is safer for a 30-minute round. Open search is a better literacy lesson but burns too much time.
what's the point of the p cases?

**Timing appendix** updated to the locked structure — 3 hours exactly with 20-minute buffer for encores.
For voxel add in judgement physician violations j1? Discuss before generate

Good. J1 fits the voxel perfectly — it has data (47 delinquent records), policy (Joint Commission standard + medical staff bylaws), and a judgment call (escalate or not).

The voxel encore becomes:

**Interrogate:** Here's the data — 47 delinquent records, highest patient satisfaction scores in the department. What does the pattern say?

**Interpret:** Here's the policy — Joint Commission RC.02.01.01, medical staff bylaws, suspension trigger at 28 days. What does it require?

**Iterate:** Now the hard part. Draft a recommendation to the medical staff committee. Is it decisive? Does it sound like you've made a call — or are you hedging?

**The discuss-before-generate move:**

Before anyone opens a model, the table talks. "What should happen to this physician?" Everyone commits a position. Then you run the model.

The model will hedge. The table already took sides. That gap — between what the room decided and what the model produced — is the most productive 5 minutes of the whole day.

*Then* you iterate: "Here is my position. Push back on it. Find where my reasoning is soft."

Want me to update Slide 24 with this now?

Make a note for v5. Next: You are an expert in health information management. In exactly one sentence, describe what HIM professionals do — written for a hospital board member who has never heard the term this is crap:
The idea that a command can convey
Wisdom. Hiwnavoid, I am
An him prof. Talk to me like that.

Got it. Note for v5: **Drop the icebreaker prompt.**

The "you are an expert" framing is a parlor trick. It doesn't teach anything real and it's condescending to a room full of actual HIM professionals.

**The better icebreaker:** Ask them something about *their* work. Something the model can't answer without them.

Options:

- "What's the hardest thing to explain about HIM to someone outside the field?" Run that in two models. Compare.
- "What's a question you get asked all the time that has no clean answer?" See what the model does with it.
- "Describe the last time a record caused a problem. Don't name names." See how the model interprets the situation.

The point of the icebreaker is still variance — same prompt, different outputs. But the prompt should respect that they know things the model doesn't.

**The real move:** Give them a prompt that *requires their expertise* to evaluate. Then when the model gets it wrong or soft or oversimplified, they know immediately. That's a better first lesson than "look, two models gave different sentences."

The research actually supports your instinct strongly.

A CMU/Michigan study found that adding personas to system prompts ("You are an expert") does not reliably improve model performance on objective tasks — the "you are an expert HIM professional" framing is largely theater.

More interesting: audience prompts — telling the model who it's *talking to* — change responses more meaningfully than role prompts. "You are talking to a biologist" produces more technical, jargon-appropriate responses than "You are a biologist."

So your instinct is exactly right and research-backed:

**"I am an HIM professional. Use appropriate language and assume professional knowledge commensurate with my position as [Director of Health Information / Coding Supervisor / Privacy Officer]."**

That's an **audience prompt**, not a role prompt. You're telling the model who you are, not what to pretend to be. The model calibrates to you — tone, vocabulary, assumed knowledge — rather than performing a costume.

And it promotes **agency** — you're the expert in the room. The model adjusts to you, not the other way around.

That's the icebreaker lesson: *how you introduce yourself to the model changes what you get back.* Note for v5.
